meta.title: "A million views means it's true": why popularity isn't proof | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to separate popularity from truth and ask "why is this right?" instead of looking at likes and views. Game-based critical thinking course for children aged 8–12.

hero.headline: Does your child think "lots of likes" = "it's true"?
hero.subheadline: "A million views — it must be true." "Everyone watches this." "Everyone does it." The numbers look like confirmation — and your child trusts the count without ever checking what's actually behind it.

media.alt: A child treating the number of likes and views as proof of truth

pain.title: Popularity isn't proof
pain.body:
Lots of people can watch, like, or repeat the same thing — but that doesn't make it true. A number shows interest, not correctness. A million views only tells you that a lot of people opened the video — and nothing about whether what's in it is true.

This isn't being naive or easily fooled. The child simply orients toward the majority, which is natural: if everyone does it, it feels like that's how it should be. Without the skill of separating content from numbers, "everyone" turns into an argument — even when there isn't a single fact behind it.

The result — the child decides under the pressure of the crowd, not the facts. They repeat, buy, and believe because "everyone does" — not because they checked whether it's actually so.

solution.body: 40 episodes, 13 critical thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually learning to protect themselves.
bullets: 🔍 Notices when a like or view count is passed off as proof
🧠 Asks "why is this right?" instead of "how many views does it have?"
💬 Understands: if everyone's into it, that still doesn't make it true
🛡️ Looks for the basis, not the numbers — and won't follow the crowd with nothing behind it

social_proof.quote: "It's got millions of views" used to be proof for my daughter. Now she asks: "But why is it actually right?" — and sees for herself that popular ≠ true.
social_proof.author: Natalia, mum of 10-year-old Sophia

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 8–12 year olds. At this age, children are most receptive to new thinking patterns and haven't yet formed rigid biases.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.

faq.q: Is registration required for the demo?
faq.a: No. The demo episode is fully open — no registration, no subscription, no personal data required.
